checks: The positive set is convex with nonempty interior, and its closure has the same interior. Compactness and boundedness give a finite integral, positive by positivity on an open set. Normalization changes the inverse power by a positive factor and rescales all masses back by the original integral. For fixed y any containing halfspace has a parallel subhalfspace through y; limiting hyperplanes are Lebesgue-null for r≥1, so dominated convergence proves joint continuity of the through-point masses.

At an exterior point a separating halfspace has zero mass; at a boundary point an outward supporting halfspace meets the support only in its Lebesgue-null hyperplane. At an interior point the local positive lower bound gives every through-point cap at least half the lower-bound ball mass. Continuity of the compact-sphere minimum therefore attains the positive global maximum in the interior of the compact support.

The active normal set is compact, as is its convex hull in finite dimension. Separation gives u·v≥δ>0 there. The shift to y*−εv changes the threshold to −εu·v; for u·v>δ/2 the added slab has the asserted thickness and offsets bounded by R/2. Its ball section actually has radius at least √3R/2, so R/2 is a valid weaker radius, and ω₀=1 makes the r=1 argument valid. The gain is at least mεδω₍ᵣ₋₁₎(R/2)ʳ⁻¹/2. Compactness of the complementary set gives a fixed gap retained under small shifts. Hence the balance holds, and deleting any zero Carathéodory coefficients yields positive weights among at most r+1 normals.

Translation preserves the hypotheses of 3919a4dbe7ace166, and p=r≥1. Since the translate is positive near zero, the parent gives a full-dimensional body with the origin interior. Dilation by r^(1/r) multiplies its radial rth power by r, which cancels the 1/r in the polar volume integral. The resulting volume is one, and integrating over each closed hemisphere gives exactly the corresponding cap probability. For r=1 the polar formula is the sum over the two directions with counting measure.

A positive balancing relation ensures at least one nonnegative scalar product for every ambient point, even if the selected normals span a proper subspace: a point orthogonal to their span is in every closed cap. Thus the same caps of mass α show that every point has depth ≤α in U, while all through-origin masses agree and give depth α there. The lower bound from 03bc771bddd39a8a applies in dimension r to U itself, without identifying the origin with its centroid.

For a closed full-dimensional simplex, the uniform density is upper semicontinuous, and the inverse power is a positive constant on the simplex and +∞ outside. Some barycentric coordinate is ≥1/(r+1) at each simplex point. Its apex cap fraction is (1−λ)^r≤(r/(r+1))^r by homothety, including zero at the apex. This independently checks the sharpness arithmetic and agrees with 03bc771bddd39a8a; r=1 gives 1/2. The uniform-body bound agrees with the original Grünbaum Theorem 2 and §3 (https://msp.org/pjm/1960/10-4/pjm-v10-n4-p18-s.pdf).

overlap.comparison: Exact constant and sharp simplex specialization for uniform convex bodies. Its uniformity hypothesis excludes nonconstant inverse-power-convex densities, which are covered here by a cap-preserving reduction. This is a strict extension, not an exact duplicate.
Ordinary maximum depth and simplex rigidity for uniform full-dimensional bodies, again only the uniform specialization.

Its Helly centerpoint argument gives the dimension-only 1/(r+1) guarantee for continuous cube-mixture marginals, without the inverse-power density condition or the sharper gamma_r bound in dimension r≥2.

summary: Balancing the minimizing normals transfers the maximum depth to a full-dimensional uniform convex body with exactly the same maximal normalized depth. The ordinary sharp bound then gives the full inverse-power density statement, with uniform simplices attaining it.
